title: Defense Wins Games
text:
Our question: Can defensive statistics in football (interceptions, fumbles forced, yards against, ect.) predict total wins in a season?
Audience: Football players who are interested in knowing which things to focus on that actually influence the amount of games they win in a season. This is important because it can help them focus on the most important things and thereby see greater improvement.
Response: Total wins in a given football season
Predictors: Yards against, interceptions, fumbles forced, points against

Show code

Our observational unit is the Xmatrix calculated above. It is basically what R will use (using its own built in ways) along with our response vector y, to estimate our \(\hat\beta\)s. Our Xmatrix has 765 rows and 5 columns. (n = 765, p = 4). Our response is y. We can see from above that our response is 765 by 1.
Our candidate predictors are “defense_n_interceptions”, “fumbles_forced”, “yards_against”, and “defense_completion_percentage”. Our response is “wins”.
The data were likely collected game by game and compiled by Score Sports Data Repository or some other organization later on. This is an observational study and not an experiment.
Evidence that the data can answer the question:
(Look for an R^2 that is fairly high to see if we can continue with the predictors and response we have chosen)

F-statistic: 174.9 on 4 and 760 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


We feel like the model is a good starting point because we pulled out as many defensive statistics as we could from our original data set. We ended with an R^2 of 0.4793. Later on we may try to find more data that corresponds with our observations that we can add to our data set to help with the low initial correlation.
Coefficient interpretation
We will interpret our \(\hat\beta\) for defense_n_interceptions. It is 0.0793 and means that, holding fumbles_forced, yards_against, and points_allowed constant, for an additional single interception on the season, number of wins predicted on the season is estimated to increase by 0.0793. The uncertainty here is that our p-value isn’t incredibly low with a \(t\) score of only 4.3. We also do not yet know if our model even passes all of the LINE assumptions.
Limitation
One limitation is that, in general, our data do not seem very correlated with our predictor. The spread of fumbles forced and wins, for example, is hardly correlated.
Pattern
There are no non-linear patterns visible from the scatter plots, however.
Improvement
An opportunity for improvement would be to find other data that correspond to the observations in our data sat so that we can increase the predictive power of our model and come up with some actually useful results.

Where the analysis could go

Possible direction: Cross Validation: It will help us see how well our data can predict run differential outside of our data. We will divide our data into test and training data and do the CV loop and evaluate average RMSEs.
Possible direction: Selection and Shrinkage: Some variables may be multi-collinear and we want to see if we can shrink our data and limit the variance on our predictor estimates. We will see what Ridge and LASSO suggest.

[1] 2.499552


We also ran a Cross Validation test to test whether this new model with the combined datasets predicts outside of itself better, which it does.

#create the cv_rmse function
library(rsample)
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data, folds) {
  results <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(folds)), function(i) {
    train <- analysis(folds$splits[[i]])
    test <- assessment(folds$splits[[i]])      #maybe somebody add some comments about what is going on here
    fit <- lm(formula, data = train)
    predictions <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
    sqrt(mean((test$wins - predictions)^2))
  })
  mean(unlist(results))
}
folds <- vfold_cv(nfl_combined, v = 5, repeats = 20)

cv_results <- data.frame(
  Model = "Model 1",
  CV_RMSE = cv_rmse(formula(nfl_mod_final), nfl_combined, folds)
)
#display results
cv_results

    Model  CV_RMSE
1 Model 1 2.519167



Changed — How we adapted our data to fit our focus:

Our AI did not seem satisfied with our predictors and data in general. So we decided to combine two datasets together so we could have more predictors that could potentially help explain our response, “wins”. We didn’t want to leave any important defensive statistics out at the beginning. That is why the model above is slightly different from the one in our AI prompt.

Rejected or corrected — AI suggestions we didn’t like:

Our AI seemed very convinced that we had a serious multicollinearity problem. Looking at the VIFs, however, there wasn’t as big of an issue as AI predicted. AI also suggested adding other defense variables. Unfortunately, including too many of the variables would make our analysis too complicated and unfocused.
Connection to the final case study:
Our observations have each football team 23 different times—because of seasons from 2000-2022. Since our AI was so concerned about independence, it suggested that we use a “Linear Mixed-Effects Model”. This model will give a random intercept for each time out of a normal distribution. AI says this model will mitigate the risk of non-independence between our observations. This extension will appear on our final page where we check the “LINE” assumptions since it will help us verify the independence assumption.

According to our AI, having a 0.8313 team variance and a 5.5012 residual variance, we can compute: ICC = 0.8313 / (0.8313 + 5.5012) ≈ 0.13. This means that about 13% of the leftover variation in wins (after accounting for the defensive stats) is stable differences between teams. AI tells us that the other 87% is season-to-season noise.
Comparison — We just saw that the independence assumption is violated, but not horribly. To test how practical this difference is, AI suggested this code:

Since the beta hats of both models are nearly the same, we are probably okay to just use our original model for the final project. Looking at SEEs would also be important for the final project.

2nd check — This time we use the “Durbin-Watson Test.”

For our second check of our Linear Mixed-effects Model we would like to do something called a “Durbin-Watson Test”. This is a test that can also look at independence. Since we concluded that independence wasn’t a big issue in part one, we want to check how accurate that claim is against another method. Here are the hypotheses of the Durbin-Watson test:
\(H_0\): There is no correlation between the residuals (the residuals are independent)
\(H_A\): The residuals are autocorrelated

But the p-value also isn’t alarmingly high. This follows very closely with how things turned out using the linear mixed model. We will definitely have to look into this more and address it in the final project.
